Sport Leicht - Lightweight luxury since 1954 

The Mercedes-Benz SL has epitomized elegance, engineering excellence, and open-top roadster luxury since the legendary 300 SL "Gullwing" (W198) debuted in 1954. SL stands for "Sport Leicht" (Sport Lightweight)—and although modern SL models are hardly featherweights, the character of a refined GT roadster has always endured. For decades, the SL-Class has served as a status symbol and the pride of the dream garage.

Generations of the MB SL

300 SL "Gullwing" & Roadster — W198 (1954–1963) 

The generation that put the SL name on the map. The 300 SL Coupé (1954–1957), with its iconic "Gullwing" doors, was the world's fastest production car at its launch and the first mass-produced car to feature fuel injection. Its successor, the 300 SL Roadster (1957–1963), switched to conventional doors but retained the same 3.0-liter inline-six engine. Extremely rare and expensive today, original Gullwings trade internationally for millions of kronor and virtually never appear on the Swedish secondary market.

The Pagoda — W113 (1963–1971)

The famous "Pagoda SL" with its concave hardtop. Designed by Paul Bracq, it is considered by many to be the most beautiful Mercedes ever built. The 230 SL, 250 SL, and 280 SL—all powered by straight-six engines. Prices have risen sharply, and well-maintained examples sell for between 700,000 and 1,500,000 SEK. California imports with automatic transmissions dominate the market.

R107 (1971–1989) 

Perhaps the most beloved SL—and certainly the most accessible classic. The R107 was produced for 18 years and is widely available. The 350 SL, 380 SL, 420 SL, and 560 SL are all popular models. The V8 engines are robust and reliable. Good-value examples can be found for under SEK 200,000, while top-tier examples with low mileage and complete documentation can reach over SEK 500,000.

R129 (1989–2001)

The most technically advanced SL at the time of its launch—featuring an automatic roll bar, ADS damping, and elegant lines. The 300 SL-24, 500 SL, and the brutal SL 600 (V12) are all represented. The SL 60 AMG is extremely rare and highly collectible. The R129 has long been undervalued, but prices have started to rise, particularly for examples with a manual transmission (a rarity).

R230 (2001–2011)

The folding steel hardtop became the SL's new signature feature. The SL 500 and SL 55 AMG (supercharged V8) are favorites. With its 500 hp, the SL 55 AMG delivers supercar performance in a refined GT package. However, the ABC (Active Body Control) suspension can be costly to repair.

R231 (2011–2020)

Lighter (featuring extensive use of aluminum in the body), sharper, and packed with technology. The lineup was topped by the SL 400 (V6 biturbo), SL 500/550 (V8 biturbo), and the brutal SL 63 AMG/SL 65 AMG (V12). The folding hardtop from the R230 returned in refined form. Magnetic shock absorbers (later updated to Magic Body Control) delivered one of the smoothest rides in the industry. A handful of extremely rare SL 65 AMG Black Series models were built—pure racing technology for the street.

R232 (2021–)

The most radical reinvention in the history of the SL. Built on the same platform as the AMG GT and now sold exclusively as the Mercedes-AMG SL—there is no longer a non-AMG variant. Features include all-wheel drive (4MATIC+) on several models, active rear-wheel steering, and a soft top instead of the previous hardtop, which saves weight. The lineup includes the SL 43 (four-cylinder turbo with electric motor), as well as the SL 55 and SL 63 (both V8 biturbo), and introduces a 2+2 layout with small rear seats for the first time since the "Pagoda." Still very rare on the Swedish used-car market, as the cars are so new.

Buying guide: Mercedes-Benz SL

What should you look out for?

- R107: Rust in the inner wheel arches, rocker panels, A-pillars, and beneath the windshield frame. Check the timing chain, automatic transmission (should shift smoothly), and A/C system (often non-functional).

- R129: The hydraulic system for the soft top is complex and expensive to repair. Check that the roof operates flawlessly. The ABC/ADS suspension system can trigger warning lights.

- R230: The ABC suspension’s hydraulic pump, accumulators, and valve block. An ABC overhaul can cost SEK 50,000–80,000. SBC brakes (Sensotronic) may also require updating.

- R231: Troubleshooting Magic Body Control sensors and air suspension can be expensive. Check that the folding hardtop opens and closes without delay or error codes.

- R232: Still under warranty for most owners—ask for the full service history and verify that all software packages (powertrain modes, driver assistance) are functioning correctly.

- General: SL cars have often sat idle for long periods—check the brake discs, rubber bushings, and cooling system extra carefully.


Recommended models/specs 


- Best value for money: R107 300/380 SL (1971–1989) — extremely reliable, simple engineering, excellent parts availability.

- The classic: W113 280 SL Pagoda — the ultimate Mercedes classic, timeless design.

- Modern GT: R230 SL 55 AMG — supercar performance, supercharged V8, superb sound.

- Rising star: R129 500 SL — undervalued, elegant, and with a fantastic V8.

- Newer tech powerhouse: R231 SL 63 AMG — V12/V8 power with modern comfort and still relatively accessible prices.

- A future classic: the R232 AMG SL 63 — an all-new platform, 2+2 layout, and all-wheel drive; likely a future collector's item.


Tip 

- An SL with both a hardtop and a soft top offers the greatest flexibility and highest value. 

- Silver/Anthracite and Signal Red metallic paints are the most timeless choices for the R107. 

- Always insist on seeing the soft top opened and closed at least twice during the test drive.
